en: NAK 1697 2/31 = NGMPP A 48/19: *Vajrasaṃbhavanāmayogavidhi*, 2 folios; the end of a *Guhyasamājoddhṛtayāgavidhi*, breaking off just before the conclusion.
The first passage is particularly interesting: it concerns the magical protection of a city; cf. GST chapter 13.72ff.

Whether in a city, or in a village, or in a district, one should apply this; by this, there will always be peace, free from all diseases. 72. (Note: This bears some superficial resemblance to Toh. 1847 (234a ff), Jinadatta’s commentary on the *Guhyasamāja-tantra*. Something has been written regarding this in Tanaka Kimiaki 1990.)
One should visualize a five-pronged vajra situated in the intermediate space; having meditated upon it as if it were the conflagration at the end of an eon, one should then command its withdrawal.
(73) Furthermore, an emanation should be performed with the radiance of the wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*); one should indeed meditate on the clouds of Dharma and then bestow the empowerment.

(74) By means of this vajra of meditation, even that which is difficult to fill becomes completely filled. (75ab) He shall become the glorious wish-fulfilling jewel, the accomplisher of the vajra of giving. (75cd)
One should cause that to radiate forth through Buddha-clouds, the great Dharmas, and Vajrasattvas; it remains for three incalculable eons and is empowered by all the Buddhas.
(76) This is the stainless secret of the body of all Buddhas. (77) This is the samādhi named "The Arising of the Vajra that Removes the Diseases of All Sentient Beings."

Visualize that those very clouds of blazing rays, as they expand, remove merely the diseases and so forth located in the city and other places—just as a cloth purified by fire removes stains—without harming the inhabitants of the city or its citizens; then see them re-entering into that very same place. This is the first application.
[The Practice:

Then, one should visualize clouds of Ratnasambhava emerging from those very same vajras, pervading the entire expanse of the sky; then, in the form of a yellow web of light rays, they enter the cities and other locations through the yoga of consecration (*abhiṣeka*) as all the Buddha-qualities. This is the second practice.
Then, one should visualize those cities and so forth pervaded by clouds of Vairocana, Amitābha, and Akṣobhya emerging from that very vajra. This is the third application.

In that regard, by the first application, the pacification of all diseases and so forth is performed. By the second, even cities and other places that were previously completely withered are thoroughly flooded. By the third, having rendered them free from all afflictions such as disease and filled with wealth, grain, and so forth, they are empowered by all the Tathāgatas and established for three eons.

Furthermore, one should meditate with a tranquil mind upon this two-pronged vajra moving through the intermediate space, which is the very nature of the Dharmakāya, stainless, and brings about peace and prosperity—either daily, at each junction of the day, or whenever appropriate—until the desired accomplishment is attained.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for sacrifice named "The Arising of the Vajra that Removes All Diseases. || 0 ||
One should contemplate the supreme Peace Mandala situated in the center of the space-element (*khadhātu*). Having meditated on the form of Vairocana, one should then place it within the heart.
(80) One should visualize the space-element as completely filled with the foremost of Locanās.

Having withdrawn [the visualization] into a mass of light rays, one should cause it to descend upon the object of commencement. The practitioner should radiate clouds of Buddhas from the openings at the tips of the pores of the skin. (81–82)
Then indeed, clouds of Buddhas bestow the consecration upon him; by this, he instantly becomes the glorious Vajrasamaya.
This is the samādhi named "The Array of Clouds of the Buddha-samaya."

Then, desiring to effect the pacification of the disease of a certain patient, the mantra-practitioner—possessing the previously described characteristics—having entered the meditation-chamber with the aforementioned features and having sat upon a comfortable seat, should place before him in a large vessel of copper or similar metal a venerable Caitya containing relics, within which are inscribed the syllables of the name of the person to be treated (sādhya) on gold or other leafy materials; above this, in a raised stand, he should place a vessel filled with water from a sacred ford mixed with white perfumes, nectar, and milk, its mouth concealed by sprouts of the mango tree or other such trees, and provided with a canopy.

Having placed the *kalaśa* [vase] [over the stūpa], one should cause a stream of blazing drops to fall upon the *uṣṇīṣa* of the stūpa, dripping from the tips of the *kuśa* grass inserted into the opening at its lower part. Then, having prepared a mandala with white sandalwood and other fragrances, having strewn it with white flowers, and having worshipped that venerable *caitya* with the five offerings, the mantra-practitioner should perform the three meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) through the yoga of Vairocana situated upon the moon within the water-mandala. Then, in his own heart, the wisdom-... [text fragment]

Having recited the mantra "Oṃ jinajik, bring peace to [Name], svāhā" upon the moon at the heart, and having produced the person to be protected by means of the first syllable of their own name, one should then place upon the moon at that heart the garland of mantra-syllables—"Oṃ ruru sphuru jvala tiṣṭha siddha locane sarvārthasādhani svāhā"—white in color, blazing, with upward-pointing heads. Then, having withdrawn the clouds of Locanā that were emanated and pervaded the expanse of space into the form of a mass of cool white rays, [one should dissolve them] into the body of the afflicted person.

One should cause [the disciple] to enter by means of the method of consecration (*abhiṣeka*). Thereafter, having emanated clouds of Vairocana from the body of the afflicted person as before, and having withdrawn them, one should cause them to enter into that very same place by means of the yoga of consecration.
By this ritual, even a sick person shall possess an indestructible and beautiful body;
before long, he shall become glorious, strong, and endowed with happiness.
Therefore, the practitioner of mantra should perform this meditation every day,
remaining perfectly composed until the disease is pacified.
Thus concludes the sacrificial ritual named "The Array of Clouds of the Buddha-Samaya. || 0 ||

Then, having thus performed the sacrifice according to the rules, on the day of the sacrifice's completion, one should perform a propitiatory *śāntika* oblation (*homa*) according to the procedure described by Homakārika, and thereafter perform the worship of the *gaṇamaṇḍala* at night.

Then, moreover, the mantra-practitioner, together with the yogins present there who have meditated upon their chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), visualizes—having moved a span’s distance above the head of the patient—the liquid of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) situated within a lunar disc, presided over by the white syllable *praṇava* (oṃ), which has become of one flavor (*samarasībhūta*) with the wisdom-nectar from the hearts of all the Tathāgatas drawn in by its rays, and which removes all aging and disease. Then, by means of a stream of flowing nectar drawn in through breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and circulated through the channels (*nāḍī*), [he pours it] into that [patient] visualized before him.

One should meditate upon the body being repeatedly offered as food, healthy and composed of vajra. Then, with the mantra *oṃ jinajik [name] śāntiṃ kuru svāhā*, one should recite it one hundred and eight times over dūrvā grass accompanied by white flowers and, preceded by a blessing, place it upon the head of the patient. Thereafter, having offered a bali-oblation to the guardians of the directions according to the instructions, one should dismiss the gaṇamaṇḍala.
The sick person who performs the entire ritual as prescribed, endowed with faith, [shall be cured].
Even one whose death is imminent,
having attained health, shall become firm of limb.
Having extracted [this] from the *Śrīsamāja* and performed the ritual procedure for me, whatever merit has been accumulated—
*kuśalaṃ yat samud[ai]...* [rest is a folio of the *Pradīpodyotana*, discovered by Tanaka, and edited by Tomabechi & Mimaki].
